Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette:
Arthur, a 58-year-old dentist with a meticulously organized practice, presented for therapy describing a life that had become constricted and colorless. Eight months prior, while driving home from a late-night study group, he was pulled over in what he later learned was a case of mistaken identity. The traffic stop escalated with bewildering speed. Confused by the officers’ aggression, he was slow to comply with their shouted commands. He was pulled from his car, and the next thing he knew, he was on the pavement, the rough asphalt scraping his cheek and the jarring sound of his own head hitting the ground echoing in his ears. The incident was over in minutes, but for Arthur, it has never ended.

In the weeks that followed, Arthur was haunted by the conviction that there was something intrinsically wrong with him, that he must have done something to provoke the violence that night. This belief that he was somehow at fault keeps the memory on a constant loop, as he endlessly replays the event, searching for the fatal error he believes he made. This rumination only makes the intrusive sounds and pains more frequent, pulling him back to the curb on that dark street. He is also consumed by a profound sense of injustice, the knowledge that his life was upended for no reason and with no accountability, which further cements his view that the world is a dangerous, unfair place.

When the memory does break through, it is not a simple recollection. Arthur hears the officer's shout as if he were standing next to him and feels a ghost of pain bloom across his cheek where it met the asphalt. The memory feels profoundly alien, like watching a film about a stranger’s humiliation, yet feeling the physical sensations in his own body. The sheer vividness of these fragments is overwhelming, confirming his deepest fear that he is losing his grip and his life has been destroyed by the trauma. The intrusion fuels his terror of the world, making every unfamiliar face, especially men, seem like a potential assailant. His response has been to shrink his world, avoiding any situation—a crowded restaurant, a tense staff meeting—that feels stressful, in a desperate attempt to keep the memories at bay.

Arthur now lives in a state of high alert. The simple act of a new patient walking into his waiting room sends a jolt of fear through him, a certainty that strangers mean harm. This persistent sense of danger forces him into a rigid set of protective behaviours; at his dental practice, he constantly scans the faces on his waiting room security monitor and has rearranged his personal office so he can always sit with his back pressed firmly into a corner, facing the only door. This hypervigilance is exhausting, and when his guard is down, the fear itself can act as a key, unlocking the memory of that night. In those moments, the raw terror convinces him all over again that he is fundamentally broken and will never be safe again.

His life has become a fortress of avoidance. He sidesteps any conversation with his partner that might lead to strong emotion, positive or negative, and has stopped reading the news entirely. This self-imposed emotional quarantine provides a fragile peace, but it also starves him of any experience that might challenge his belief that his life has been irrevocably destroyed. He has trouble sleeping most nights, lying awake for hours scanning the dark for threats. Furthermore, this numb existence makes the memories, when they inevitably breach his defenses, feel all the more shocking and bizarre, reinforcing the sense that they are happening to someone else. He came to therapy after his partner of twenty years told him the silence in their home had become unbearable. Arthur feels trapped, exhausted by the constant effort of keeping himself safe from a world he no longer trusts and from a memory that feels both intimately his and horribly foreign.
